title: This is what a supercar was like a century ago
gist: A passenger ride at Laguna Seca in "Smoky" (YM 4037), the 12th of just 18 Bentley Super Sports built between 1925 and 1927, used by Bentley during Monterey Car Week to tie its new Supersports to a century-old heritage nameplate. The original guaranteed more than 100 mph when a Ford Model T struggled to reach 40, and the car later won seven races at Brooklands after a 4.5 L Le Mans-winning engine swap.

insights.claim: Bentley brought a privately owned 1926 Super Sports to Laguna Seca alongside its new Supersports model during Monterey Car Week, staffing it with its heritage department to link the modern car to a nameplate first used a century earlier.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Luxury automakers monetize provenance directly; an in-house heritage fleet is a marketing asset that supports pricing power on limited-run modern cars.

insights.claim: Bentley built only 18 Super Sports between 1925 and 1927 by taking the standard 3 Litre model and shortening the wheelbase by 9.5 inches, shaving mass and adding a more tapered, lower-drag radiator.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Extreme scarcity of the historical run is what makes the badge revivable at premium prices a hundred years later.
insights.locator: Bentley built 18 Super Sports between 1925 and 1927

insights.claim: The original Super Sports used a specially built 3.0 L engine with new pistons, a lighter flywheel, higher compression and different carburetors, and the factory guaranteed it would exceed 100 mph at a time when the millions of Ford Model Ts on the road were hard-pushed to break 40 mph.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A 2.5x performance gap over the mass-market car of the era is the same structural positioning premium marques still rely on today.
insights.locator: Like today with the Continental GT

insights.claim: In 1925-27 the bodywork on a Bentley was still a matter of whichever coachbuilder the owner chose, with this particular car wearing two-seater bodywork from Jarvis of Wimbledon.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The rolling-chassis-plus-coachbuilder model is the historical precedent for today's platform-and-customization strategies in ultra-luxury automotive.

insights.claim: Smoky's second owner, Bentley racing driver Kit Baker-Carr, swapped in a 4.5 L motor from the car that won Le Mans in 1928 and used it to take seven wins at Brooklands between 1935 and 1937, with a fastest lap of almost 117 mph.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Documented competition history and a Le Mans-winning engine are the provenance attributes that command the highest multiples in the collector-car market.

insights.claim: The car has no safety belts or roll bars, the three-speed transmission lever sits outside the body, and the pedal layout is inverted from modern practice with the accelerator in the middle and the brake on the right — reportedly because brakes were so ineffective in period racing.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A reminder of how much of modern vehicle safety and control layout is regulatory convention rather than engineering necessity, and how fast such standards can be rewritten.
insights.quote: Not sure the FIA or NHTSA would let you get away with that today.
insights.locator: Get in, let’s go for a ride

insights.claim: On the ride the author found the 19-inch tires had more cornering grip than expected and that most of the audible noise came as a whine from the gearbox rather than from the engine, despite heavy buffeting from the small screens.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: First-hand assessments of vintage dynamic capability feed collector sentiment, which is where valuations for cars like this are actually set.
insights.locator: What I didn’t expect was the cornering grip
